text: Looping over cursor rows by hand was fine for a quick test, but it's not how you'll actually pull data day to day. pd.read_sql takes a query and hands you back a DataFrame directly.

Point read_sql at any connection and any query, and you get a DataFrame back with column types already inferred -- no manual loop building lists of tuples. This query pulls the top ten AdventureWorks2012 products by list price.

Here's the real power move: join tables inside the SQL itself. This joins SalesOrderHeader, SalesOrderDetail, and Product -- three real AdventureWorks2012 tables -- entirely inside SQL Server, before any of it reaches pandas.

You could pull all three tables into pandas separately and merge them yourself, but that drags far more data across the network than you need. For genuinely large tables -- hundreds of thousands of rows -- chunksize turns read_sql into an iterator of smaller DataFrames instead of one giant one.

Push the join down to SQL whenever the database can see all the tables involved. It means less data moving across the network, less work for pandas to do afterward, and it plays to the database engine's actual strength.
Notice none of these queries spliced in a user-supplied value -- that's not an accident, and Lesson 29 explains exactly why. Next up: writing data back into the database, not just reading it out.
